title: Last Stone Weight
summary: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones: equal ones both vanish, otherwise the lighter vanishes and the heavier loses that weight. Return the last stone's weight, or 0.
statement:
Each element of `stones` is the weight of a stone. Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones, with weights `x ≤ y`, and smash them together:

- if `x == y`, both stones are destroyed,
- otherwise the lighter stone is destroyed and the heavier one now weighs `y − x`.

When at most one stone is left, return its weight, or `0` if none remain.
hints: You need the two largest values over and over, while the collection changes.
A max-heap (PriorityQueue with a reversed comparator) gives you the largest in O(log n).
Poll two, push back the difference if it is non-zero, and repeat while the heap has at least two stones.
explain: Smash 8 and 7 (leaves 1), then 4 and 2 (leaves 2), then 2 and 1 (leaves 1), then 1 and 1 (nothing). One stone of weight 1 remains, so the answer is 1.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
summary: KthLargest(k, nums) starts with some values; each add(val) adds a value to the stream and returns the k-th largest so far.

perf.label: 10,000 adds, k = 5,000
perf.call: KthLargest kl = new KthLargest(5000, BCB.ints(10000, -10000, 10000)); long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) sum += kl.add(BCB.rnd(-10000, 10000)); Object r = sum;

statement:
Design `KthLargest`, which tracks the `k`-th largest value in a stream of numbers (in sorted order, so duplicates count):

- `KthLargest(int k, int[] nums)` starts with the values in `nums`,
- `int add(int val)` adds `val` to the stream and returns the current `k`-th largest value.

`add` is only called when at least `k` values exist after adding. The tests call the class with a list of operations and their arguments.
hints: You do not need all the values, only the k largest ones.
Keep a min-heap of size k: its smallest element is the k-th largest overall.
On add, push the value and pop while the heap has more than k elements; then return the top.
explain: With `k = 3`, each `add` returns the 3rd largest value so far. After adding 3 the top three are 8, 5, 4 (answer 4); after 5 it is 5; after 10 it is 5; after 9 and 4 it is 8. Output: `[null,4,5,5,8,8]`.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
summary: Return the k-th largest element (in sorted order, so duplicates count) — try to beat a full sort.
statement:
Return the `k`-th largest element of `nums`. This means the `k`-th element in sorted (descending) order, not the `k`-th distinct value, so duplicates count.

Sorting is O(n log n). Try to do better.

For example in `[3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6]` with `k = 4` the answer is 4: the two 5s count separately. A min-heap holding the `k` largest values seen so far gives O(n log k).
hints: A min-heap holding the k largest values seen so far gives O(n log k).
Quickselect partitions around a pivot like quicksort but only recurses into the side that contains position n − k: average O(n).
Pick a random pivot (or use three-way partitioning) so arrays with many equal values or already-sorted input do not degrade to O(n²). Since values are small, counting sort is also O(n).
explain: Sorted from largest, the values are 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. The 2nd largest is 5.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
summary: Return the k most frequent values (the answer is unique), in any order — better than O(n log n) if you can.

perf.label: 80,200 values, k = 50
perf.gen: List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(); for (int v = 1; v <= 400; v++) for (int c = 0; c < v; c++) l.add(v); Collections.shuffle(l, BCB.R); int[] a0 = l.stream().mapToInt(x -> x).toArray(); int a1 = 50;

statement:
Return the `k` values that occur most often in `nums`, in any order.

The answer is unique: there is no tie at the boundary. Try to beat O(n log n).

Count the values first, then pick the `k` with the highest counts, with a heap of size `k` or by bucketing values by their count.
hints: Start by counting each value with a HashMap.
A min-heap of size k ordered by count keeps the k most frequent values: O(n log k).
For O(n), use bucket sort: bucket[c] lists the values that occur c times. Walk the buckets from the highest count down until you have k values.
explain: 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears twice and 3 once. The 2 most frequent values are 1 and 2, so the answer is `[1,2]` (in any order).

title: K Closest Points to Origin
summary: Return the k points closest to (0, 0) by Euclidean distance, in any order.

perf.label: 10,000 points
perf.gen: int[] p = BCB.perm(10000, 0); int[][] a0 = new int[10000][]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = new int[] { p[i], 0 }; int a1 = 2000;

statement:
`points[i] = [x, y]` is a point on the plane. Return the `k` points closest to the origin `(0, 0)` by Euclidean distance, in any order.

The answer is unique for every test (no ties at the boundary).

Comparing squared distances is enough, since the square root doesn't change the order.
hints: Compare squared distances x² + y²; the square root does not change the order.
A max-heap of size k, ordered by distance, keeps the k closest points seen so far: pop the farthest whenever it grows past k.
Quickselect on the distances gives average O(n).
explain: The squared distances are 1² + 3² = 10 for `[1,3]` and 2² + 2² = 8 for `[-2,2]`. The closest point is `[-2,2]`, so the answer is `[[-2,2]]`.

title: Task Scheduler
summary: Each task (a letter) takes one interval, and two runs of the same task must be at least n intervals apart (idle is allowed). Return the fewest intervals to finish all tasks.
statement:
`tasks` lists CPU tasks, each named by an uppercase letter. Each task takes one interval. In every interval the CPU either runs one task or stays idle.

Two runs of the same task must be separated by at least `n` intervals. Tasks can run in any order. Return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all of them.
hints: The most frequent task decides the shape: its runs must be spread out with n slots in between.
If the highest count is maxCount and m tasks share it, the frame (maxCount − 1) × (n + 1) + m is a lower bound.
The answer is max(tasks.length, that frame): if there are enough other tasks, no idle slots are needed at all.
explain: With a cooldown of 2, the same task can't run in back-to-back slots or with one slot between. The best order is A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A, B: 8 intervals.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
summary: Rows and columns of an n×n matrix are sorted ascending. Return the k-th smallest value overall (duplicates count).
statement:
`matrix` is `n × n`, and both every row and every column are sorted in ascending order. Return the `k`-th smallest value in the whole matrix, counting duplicates.

Try to use less than O(n²) memory.

Duplicates count: the two 13s are the 7th and 8th smallest. The matrix can be treated as `n` sorted lists merged with a heap, or searched by value.
hints: Each row is a sorted list, so this is like merging n sorted lists and stopping at the k-th value.
A min-heap seeded with the first element of each row, popping k times and pushing the next element of the same row, takes O(k log n).
Alternatively binary-search on the value: count how many entries are ≤ mid by walking a staircase from the bottom-left corner in O(n).
explain: The values in sorted order are 1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 15. The 8th of them is 13.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
summary: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list and return it.

perf.label: 1,000 lists of 100 nodes
perf.gen: ListNode[] a0 = new ListNode[1000]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = BCBN.of(BCB.sorted(100, -1000000, 1000000));

statement:
`lists` holds `k` linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.

Some lists may be empty, and `lists` itself may be empty.

Reuse the existing nodes by relinking them; there's no need to create new ones. A min-heap of the current front nodes always gives the next smallest.
constraints: Each list is sorted in ascending order
hints: Merging lists one at a time into a growing result repeats work: O(k · N).
Keep the current head of every list in a min-heap. Repeatedly take the smallest node, append it, and push its successor.
That is O(N log k) for N nodes in total. Merging lists in pairs, like merge sort, has the same complexity.
explain: Repeatedly taking the smallest front node of the three lists gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, so the merged list is `[1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]`.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
summary: MedianFinder supports addNum(num) and findMedian(), the median of all numbers added so far (the mean of the two middle values when the count is even).

perf.label: 50,000 adds, each followed by findMedian
perf.call: MedianFinder mf = new MedianFinder(); double sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 50000; i++) { mf.addNum(BCB.rnd(-100000, 100000)); sum += mf.findMedian(); } Object r = sum;

statement:
Design `MedianFinder`:

- `MedianFinder()` creates an empty structure,
- `void addNum(int num)` adds a number,
- `double findMedian()` returns the median of all numbers added so far: the middle value, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even.

`findMedian` is only called after at least one `addNum`. Answers within `10^-5` are accepted. The tests call the class with a list of operations and their arguments.
hints: Keeping a sorted list costs O(n) per insert. You only ever need the middle.
Use two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half.
After each insert, rebalance so the max-heap has the same size as the min-heap or one more. The median is the max-heap top, or the average of both tops.
explain: After adding 1 and 2 the median is the average of the two middle values, 1.5. After adding 3 the values are 1, 2, 3 and the median is 2.0. Output: `[null,null,null,1.5,null,2.0]`.

title: IPO
summary: You start with capital w and may finish at most k projects; project i needs capital[i] to start and adds profits[i]. Return the largest final capital.
statement:
You start with capital `w` and may complete at most `k` distinct projects, one after another. Project `i` can only be started if your current capital is at least `capital[i]`; finishing it adds `profits[i]` to your capital.

Return the largest capital you can have at the end.
hints: Capital never decreases, so the set of projects you can afford only grows over time.
Greedily pick, each round, the most profitable project you can currently afford.
Sort projects by required capital. Each round, push every newly affordable project's profit into a max-heap, then take the top. Stop early if the heap is empty.
explain: With capital 0 only project 0 is affordable: finishing it raises capital to 1. Then the best affordable project is project 2 (profit 3), bringing capital to 4 after the 2 allowed projects.

title: Single-Threaded CPU
summary: tasks[i] = [enqueueTime, processingTime]. A single CPU, whenever idle, starts the available task with the shortest processing time (smallest index on ties) and runs it to completion. Return the order in which tasks are processed.

perf.label: n = 100,000
perf.gen: int[][] a0 = new int[100000][]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = new int[] { BCB.rnd(1, 1000000000), BCB.rnd(1, 20000) };

hints: Simulate time. Sort the task indices by enqueue time so you can add newly available tasks in order.
Keep the available tasks in a min-heap ordered by (processing time, index). Whenever the CPU is free, pop the top.
If the heap is empty, jump the clock forward to the next enqueue time instead of ticking one unit at a time. Use a 64-bit clock: total processing time can reach 10¹⁴.
explain: At time 1 only task 0 is available, so it runs until time 3. Tasks 1 and 2 are waiting; task 2 is shorter, so it runs until 5. Then task 3 (time 1) beats task 1 (time 4). The order is `[0,2,3,1]`.

title: Reorganize String
summary: Rearrange the letters of s so that no two adjacent letters are equal, and return any such arrangement, or "" if none exists.
statement:
Rearrange the characters of `s` so that no two adjacent characters are the same. Return any valid arrangement, or `""` if it is impossible.

For example "aaab" is impossible: three a's in four characters always leaves two of them side by side, so the answer there is "".
hints: When is it impossible? Think about the most frequent letter: it needs a different letter between every two of its copies.
It is possible exactly when the highest count is at most ⌈n / 2⌉, that is (n + 1) / 2 in integer division.

Place the most frequent letter at indices 0, 2, 4, …, then keep filling the remaining even indices and wrap around to the odd ones with the other letters. Alternatively, greedily take the two most frequent letters from a max-heap each round.
explain: "a" appears twice in a string of length 3, which is allowed (at most ⌈3 / 2⌉ = 2). Putting the a's at positions 0 and 2 and the b between them gives "aba".

title: Longest Happy String
summary: Build the longest string using at most a letters "a", b letters "b" and c letters "c" that never contains "aaa", "bbb" or "ccc". Return any longest one ("" if none).
statement:
A string is **happy** if it contains only the letters `"a"`, `"b"` and `"c"` and never contains `"aaa"`, `"bbb"` or `"ccc"` as a substring.

Given `a`, `b` and `c`, return the **longest** happy string that uses at most `a` letters `"a"`, at most `b` letters `"b"` and at most `c` letters `"c"`. If several are equally long, return any of them. If none exists, return `""`.
hints: Greedy: at every step, try to use the letter you have the most of left, because that is the one most likely to be stranded.
If the last two letters you wrote are already that letter, use the letter with the second-highest count instead (if any remain).
Stop when neither choice is possible. A max-heap of (count, letter), or simply sorting three counts each step, finds the top two.
explain: There are many more c's than anything else, so each pair of c's needs another letter after it. Writing cc, a, cc, b, cc uses all the a and b letters; one more c would make "ccc". The result "ccaccbcc" has length 8, the most possible.
